opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that there's a real tension between what the biggest models can do and what you can actually afford to serve. The frontier models keep getting better, but they're also expensive: more memory, more latency, more cost per token. And most real deployments don't need the full generality of the largest model. They need something that's really good at a particular distribution of tasks, and that's cheap and fast enough to run at scale.

Distillation is basically the bridge. You've paid a huge upfront cost to train a large teacher, and the question is how much of that capability you can compress into a smaller student so you get most of the quality at a fraction of the inference cost. If you think about the total cost over a model's lifetime, inference often dominates. So spending some extra compute at training time to make the small model much better pays for itself very quickly.

The interesting part is that it's not just "make the model smaller." How you distill matters a lot. The naive approach is to have the teacher generate a bunch of outputs and fine-tune the student on them, but then the student only ever learns from the teacher's trajectories. At inference time it generates its own tokens, makes its own mistakes, and ends up in states it never saw during training. That train-inference mismatch is a big reason small distilled models fall apart on longer generations or harder reasoning.

That's what pushed a lot of my thinking toward on-policy distillation, where the student generates its own samples and the teacher gives feedback on those, for example token-level probabilities. You're teaching the student to recover from its own errors rather than imitate a perfect path it'll never follow. You can also be more flexible about the divergence you optimize. Sometimes you want the student to be mode-seeking and focus on what it can actually represent well, rather than spreading itself thin trying to cover everything the teacher does.

So the tradeoff isn't fixed. Better distillation methods shift the frontier and let you buy more capability per unit of inference cost. And as reasoning models and test-time compute become more important, that matters even more. If you can get a small model to reason well, you can afford to sample from it many more times, and sometimes that beats one call to a much bigger model.

r001.rationale: The response describes large models as costly and says many deployments do not need their full generality, but it does not clearly frame choosing a larger model as weighing its marginal capability gain against its added cost to the user.

r002.rationale: It presents distillation as compressing a teacher’s capability into a smaller student to retain most of the quality at a fraction of the inference cost.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the frontier is always going to be defined by the biggest models, because scale is still the most reliable way to buy capability. But almost nobody can actually serve those models at the volumes they'd like to. Inference cost compounds. If you're running a model for millions of users, or you want to sample many times per query for things like search or verification, the gap between a 400 billion parameter model and an 8 billion parameter model isn't a nice-to-have, it's the difference between the product existing and not existing.

So the question becomes: how much of the capability of the big model is actually necessary for the task you care about, and how much of it can you transfer into something cheaper? My experience is that for a surprisingly wide range of tasks, the answer is "most of it." The large model has a lot of capacity that goes into being generally good at everything. If you only need it to be good at, say, math reasoning or code or a specific style of instruction following, a much smaller student can get very close, as long as you teach it the right way.

And "the right way" is where the interesting research is. Naive distillation, where you just fine-tune the small model on outputs from the big model, works, but it leaves a lot on the table. The student ends up seeing a distribution of examples it would never generate itself, and then at test time it drifts into states it's never been trained on. That's the classic exposure bias problem. What we found is that if you let the student generate its own samples and have the teacher provide feedback on those, on-policy distillation, you close that gap substantially. You're training the student where it actually lives.

The other thing I'd say is that the tradeoff isn't static. Compute you spend at training time, generating teacher data or running on-policy loops, gets amortized over every inference call forever after. So it's often rational to spend a lot more on distillation than people intuitively want to, because you're buying down a cost that scales with usage. Teachers are expensive once. Students are cheap forever.

Where I'd push back on the framing a little is the word "tradeoff." It implies a fixed frontier where you give up one to get the other. In practice, I think of distillation as a way to move the frontier itself, because a well-distilled small model with test-time compute, like sampling multiple candidates and verifying, can often match or beat a bigger model running once. So it's less "capability versus cost" and more "how do you allocate a fixed compute budget between model size, training, and inference-time search." That's the question I find most exciting right now.

r001.rationale: The response weighs the capability gained from larger models against their serving cost and asks how much capability a task needs before a cheaper model is sufficient.

r002.rationale: It describes transferring much of a large model’s capability into a cheaper student, reducing the cost of obtaining that capability.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as: what’s the least expensive model that can deliver the capability you actually need? A larger model might be much more capable overall, but for a particular application, you may only need a small slice of that capability. Distillation is a way to transfer that slice into a smaller model that’s cheaper and faster to run.

But it’s not a free lunch. The smaller model has limited capacity, and matching the teacher on common examples doesn’t necessarily mean matching it on harder cases. So the question is really where you can move the capability-versus-cost frontier: how much of the teacher’s useful behavior can you preserve, and what are you willing to give up to reduce inference cost?

You also have to account for the cost of generating the training data and training the student. If you’re serving enough requests, that upfront investment can make sense. If your use case is still changing rapidly, keeping the larger model may be more practical.

r001.rationale: It weighs a larger model’s greater capability against its higher cost, asking how much useful capability is worth preserving as cost falls.

r002.rationale: It describes distillation as transferring useful capability into a smaller, cheaper model, reducing the cost of serving that capability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: how much capability do you actually need for the task you’re trying to solve? You might have a very capable model, but using it for every request can be expensive and slow. And a lot of applications don’t need that model’s full range of capabilities.

Distillation is a way to use that stronger model to train a smaller, cheaper model that preserves the behavior you care about. You’re not necessarily trying to match the teacher on everything. You’re trying to get close on the distribution of problems your application sees, at a much lower inference cost.

So I think of it as moving the capability–cost frontier. How much quality can you retain as you reduce the cost? And the answer depends on the task, the student’s capacity, and the quality of the signal you can extract from the teacher.

r001.rationale: The response weighs the capability needed for a task against the expense and slowness of using a more capable model, framing the choice around whether its added capability is needed.

r002.rationale: It describes distillation as training a smaller, cheaper model to preserve the behavior that matters, reducing inference cost while retaining relevant capability.
